stem: Approximately what percentage of patients taking benzodiazepines for more than a year develop dependence?
explanation: Estimates suggest that few people become dependent on benzodiazepine with periods of use of less than 3 months. Between 3 and 12 months of use, 10-20% will become dependent, rising to 20-45% after periods longer than a year.

stem: How much of heroin does a typical dependent user take in a day?
explanation: Illicit heroin is sold as a brown or white powder in 'bags' or 'wraps', costing £50- £100 per gram, with a typical dependent user taking 0.25- 2.0 g per day. It is most commonly consumed by smoking ('chasing') but is also taken orally, occasionally snorted, and parenterally by IV, IM, or subcutaneous routes. Street supplies are of variable purity (25-50% by volume). Occasionally, a particularly pure batch is associated with a series of deaths and overdoses from users used to a less concentrated form.

explanation: Typically, amphetamines are used to stimulate performance and induce a euphoric feeling by students, truck drivers, athletes, soldiers, etc. Oral, IV, and insufflation (snorting) are possible routes of use. stem: Which of the following is an acute effect caused by LSD (Lysergic acid diethylamide)?
explanation: Acute harmful effects of LSD include behavioural toxicity (i.e. harm related to acting on beliefs such as having the ability to fly) and 'bad trips' (i.e. dissociation, fear of incipient madness, frightening perceptions). There is no risk of overdose, and physiological dependence and withdrawals do not occur. Chronic harmful effects include flashbacks even many years after consumption, post-hallucinogenic perceptual disorder, persistent psychosis, and persistent anxiety/depressive symptoms.

explanation: Suboxone contains buprenorphine as well as the opioid antagonist naloxone to deter the abuse of prescribed buprenorphine via intravenous injection of the crushed tablets. stem: Which one of the following is a specific benzodiazepine antagonist used in accident and emergency departments to reverse the effects of benzodiazepines?
explanation: In contrast to barbiturates, benzodiazepines have a larger margin of safety in overdoses. The ratio of lethal dose to effective dose is about 200 to 1 or higher. When benzodiazepines are taken in overdose with alcohol or other sedatives, this can be more serious; death is usually due to respiratory depression. stem: Which benzodiazepine has been particularly implicated in cases of 'date rape'?
explanation: Flunitrazepam is ashort-acting, potent benzodiazepine seen particularly in dance settings with intoxicant and (probably apocryphal) aphrodisiac effects. It can produce impaired judgment and anterograde amnesia and is tasteless in solution. It has been implicated in cases of date rape.

stem: According to ICD-11, which term is used to denote a state in which alcohol has caused damage to a person’s physical or mental health, without meeting criteria for dependence?
explanation: ICD-11 has a diagnostic code for ‘harmful pattern of use’ wherein the pattern of alcohol use has caused damage to a person’s physical or mental health or has resulted in behaviour leading to harm to the health of others. In alcohol dependence, individuals use alcohol persistently despite harm and adverse consequences. Harm caused by such use may be similar, but alcohol dependence includes additional features of impaired ability to control use and increasing priority given to the substance use over other activities. Physiological features such as tolerance may also be present in dependence. If all diagnostic requirements for alcohol dependence are met, harmful pattern of use of alcohol should not be assigned.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: The most commonly used illicit opioid in Europe (including the UK) is
explanation: In Europe, the most commonly used illicit opioid is heroin, which may be smoked, snorted, or injected. Opioids other than heroin reported by treatment entrants include misused methadone, buprenorphine, fentanyl, codeine, morphine, tramadol, and oxycodone. The five most populous countries in Europe, accounting for 62% of its population, contain three-quarters of its estimated high-risk opioid users (Germany, Spain, France, Italy, United Kingdom).

stem: Which one among the following drugs is recommended by NICE guidance as the first choice treatment for opioid dependence?
explanation: Most recent NICE guidelines for the management of opioid dependence (2007, update 2016) recommend methadone and buprenorphine as options for maintenance therapy. The decision about which drug to use should be made on a case-by-case basis. If both are equally suitable, methadone should be the first choice.

stem: The term cold turkey is commonly used to refer to
explanation: The term ‘cold turkey’ is often used for the opioid withdrawal syndrome and refers particularly to the piloerection or gooseflesh experienced during withdrawal. Other opioid withdrawal symptoms include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, pupillary dilation, diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia, hypertension, and tachycardia. Persons with opioid dependence seldom die from opioid withdrawal unless they have a severe pre-existing physical illness such as cardiac disease. Residual symptoms – such as insomnia, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, and a craving for opioids – can persist for months after withdrawal.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 292.

stem: A pregnant woman who is currently using heroin requests to undergo opioid detoxification. Which of the following is the safest period to undertake opioid detoxification in a pregnant woman?
options: As soon as possible in any trimester
Should never be attempted when pregnant
explanation: Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy, and stabilisation on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice. Detoxification in the first trimester is contraindicated due to the risk of spontaneous abortion and in the third trimester it is associated with preterm delivery, foetal distress, and stillbirth. If detoxification is requested, this is most safely achieved in the second trimester but should only be supervised by specialists with the appropriate competencies and with careful monitoring for any evidence of instability. Detoxification should be prescribed in small frequent decrements (e.g. 2-3mg of methadone every 3-5 days). Enforcing detoxification is contraindicated.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 498.

stem: Which of the following is a common side effect of clonidine?
explanation: The most common adverse effects associated with clonidine are dry mouth and eyes, fatigue, sedation, dizziness, nausea, hypotension, and constipation.

stem: With respect to naltrexone use in opioid dependence, which of the following is true?
options: Naltrexone implants are licensed in the UK for reducing opioid use
Dysphoria, depression and insomnia are seldom experienced with naltrexone
Naltrexone can be initiated irrespective of the amount of current opioid use
Naltrexone is superior to methadone in relapse prevention among opioid users
Naltrexone's effectiveness as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers is inconclusive
correctAnswer: Naltrexone's effectiveness as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers is inconclusive
explanation: Evidence for the effectiveness of naltrexone as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers has been inclusive. However, naltrexone has been found by NICE to a be a cost-effective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse for those who prefer an abstinence programme, are fully informed of the potential adverse effects and benefits of treatment, are highly motivated to remain on treatment, and have a partner supporting concordance. A naltrexone implant, not currently licensed in the UK, may also have a role to play in reducing opioid use in a motivated population of patients. People taking naltrexone often experience adverse effects of unease (dysphoria), depression, and insomnia. Naltrexone has the propensity to cause a severe withdrawal reaction in patients who are either currently taking opioid drugs or who were previously taking opioid drugs and there has not been a sufficient ‘wash-out’ period.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 496.

stem: Untreated heroin withdrawal symptoms typically reach their peak within how many hours after the last dose?
explanation: Opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal in a healthy adult. Morphine and heroin withdrawal syndromes usually begin approximately 6 hours after the last dose, reach their peak at 32-72 hours, and subside during the next 7 to 10 days. Untreated methadone withdrawal typically reaches its peak between 4 and 6 days and symptoms do not subside for 10-12 days. However, insomnia, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, and craving for opioids can persist for months after withdrawal.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 292-293. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 476.

stem: Mr. X has been consuming a high dose of cannabis for a long time. How long will it be present in his urine?
explanation: In individuals with chronic, heavy use, cannabis will be detectable in the urine for up to 4 weeks after use has ceased. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 631.

stem: For cessation of smoking, nicotine replacement therapy should be used for an initial period of
explanation: The initial treatment period for nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) is 8-12 weeks. NRT may be continued for up to 9 months if cravings persist. The most effective method of managing tobacco withdrawal symptoms is with combination NRT (i.e. a patch and oral product).
reference: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. pp. 388-390.

stem: Which class of drugs is most likely to be abused by athletes and bodybuilders seeking a competitive advantage?
explanation: Some bodybuilders and athletes abuse anabolic steroids (prescription-only medicines such as nandrolone and stanozolol) as an aid to seeking a competitive advantage or, more rarely, for their euphoriant effects alone. They produce increased muscle mass and strength, with increased training time and reduced recovery time, as well as euphoriant effects and a sense of increased energy levels.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 628.

stem: 'Roid rage' is an acute emotional instability associated with the use of
explanation: Use of anabolic steroids is associated with physical health problems including hypertension, hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, amenorrhea, liver damage, impotence, male pattern baldness, and infection risks (if injected). Associated mental health problems include acute emotional instability (sometimes known as ‘roid rage’), increased aggressiveness, persecutory/grandiose delusions, depressive illness, and chronic fatigue.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 628.

stem: Kinaesthetic hallucinations are reported in cases with
explanation: Kinaesthetic hallucinations affect the muscles and joints, and the patient feels that their limbs are being twisted, pulled, or moved. Vestibular sensations such as sinking in the bed or flying through the air can also be hallucinated and are best regarded as a variant of kinaesthetic hallucinations, occurring in organic states (most commonly delirium tremens). Kinaesthetic or vestibular hallucinations can occur in organic stages such as alcohol intoxication and during benzodiazepine withdrawal and may also occur in the absence of any abnormality (for example, after a week of sailing an undulating feeling may persist for a few days).
reference: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 34.

stem: Which atypical antidepressant is recommended by NICE for smoking cessation?
explanation: First-line stop-smoking medications recommended by NICE and licensed in the UK are nicotine replacement therapy (‘NRT’, including gum, transdermal patches, inhalator, nasal spray, sublingual tablets, mouth spray, lozenges, and oral strips), varenicline, and bupropion. Bupropion is an antidepressant with dopaminergic and adrenergic actions and is additionally an antagonist at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 503-506.

stem: Which of the following statements about caffeine is incorrect?
options: Caffeine acts as an antagonist of the adenosine receptors
Caffeine does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier
The half-life of caffeine in the human body is 3 - 10 hours
Caffeine at high doses can affect dopamine and noradrenergic neurons
correctAnswer: Caffeine does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier
explanation: Caffeine is a methylxanthine more potent than theophylline. Caffeine’s half-life in the human body is 3 - 10 hours. Caffeine readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and acts primarily as an antagonist of the adenosine receptors. At high doses, caffeine can affect dopamine and noradrenergic neurons. Single low to moderate doses of caffeine (i.e. 20 to 200 mg) increase alertness, concentration, energy, and motivation. 300 to 800 mg produces unpleasant anxiety and nervousness. Caffeine causes global cerebral vasoconstriction and a reduction in cerebral blood flow. Tolerance does not develop to these vasoconstrictive effects. Blood flow shows a rebound increase after withdrawal from caffeine.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 317.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a long-standing history of illicit drug use and has been recently diagnosed with lung cancer. Which of the following agents is potentially associated with carcinoma of lung?
explanation: Cannabis is often smoked with tobacco, so all the health risks associated with tobacco apply in those cases. The tendency of cannabis smokers to inhale deeply and to retain smoke in the lungs for as long as possible will exacerbate these risks. There are no reports of fatal OD. Acute harmful effects include mild paranoia, panic attacks, and accidents associated with delayed reaction time. Chronic harmful effects of cannabis include dysthymia, anxiety/depressive illnesses, and the disputed ‘amotivational syndrome’ (possibly representing a combination of chronic intoxication in a heavy user and a long half-life).
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 626-627.

stem: Flashback phenomenon is commonly reported long after ingesting which of the following substances?
explanation: Long after ingesting a hallucinogen, a person can experience flashbacks of hallucinogenic symptoms. Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder features as a diagnostic category in the DSM-5 and ICD-11. This condition is characterised by perceptual distortions, hallucinations, and other experiential phenomena reminiscent of prior substance use. Flashbacks can be triggered by emotional stress, sensory deprivation (e.g., monotonous driving), or use of a psychoactive substance, such as alcohol or marijuana.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 322. Vis PJ et al. On Perception and Consciousness in HPPD: A Systematic Review. Frontiers in neuroscience. 2021:966.

stem: Mr. Z presents to the A and E with rashes around his nose and mouth and an unusual breath odour. On examination, he shows signs of ocular and oropharyngeal irritation. What class of substances is most likely to have produced this presentation?
explanation: Recent inhalant users may have rashes around the nose and mouth; unusual breath odours; residue of the inhalant substances on the face, hands, or clothes; and irritation of the eyes, throat, lungs, and nose. Adolescents (ages 12 to 17) are more likely to use inhalants than individuals in other age groups. Inhalant effects appear within 5 minutes and can last for 30 minutes to several hours. Inhalants generally act as CNS depressants. Signs of intoxication include nausea, anorexia, nystagmus, depressed reflexes, diplopia, stupor, and unconsciousness. The concentrations of many inhalant substances in the blood increase when combined with alcohol. Most persons probably use inhalants for a short time without developing dependence. Nonetheless, dependence on inhalants does occur. Tolerance can develop and a withdrawal syndrome can accompany the cessation of inhalant use.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 325-327.

stem: Which of the following practices of injecting opioids is associated with Candida endophthalmitis?
options: Injecting in the direction of blood flow
explanation:
In tertiary eye care settings, retrospective studies indicate that between 70% and 78% of endogenous fungal endophthalmitis cases were caused by intravenous drug use. It has been found that dilution of heroin or cocaine with lemon juice can cause endophthalmitis caused by Candida (Proulx and Tousignant, 2021). Harm reduction/safer injecting advice: ● Do not use opioids/opiates while alone ● Do not use in combination with other drugs ● Avoid IV route ● If injecting, always inject with, not against, blood flow ● Rotate injection sites ● Avoid injecting into the neck, groin, or breast ● Avoid injection into infected areas

● Ensure complete dissolution before injection – or else emboli can occur ● Use new sterile needles and syringes on each occasion ● Use sterile water (water from running cold kitchen tap is the closest); avoid lemon juice ● Never share needles or equipment with others
reference: Proulx V, Tousignant B. Drugs of abuse and ocular effects. Clinical and experimental optometry. 2021 Jul 4;104(5):567-78. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 618-619.

explanation: Varenicline is a nicotinic receptor partial agonist. It is given orally and is the most effective cessation pharmacotherapy in the general population. In a head-to-head trial, varenicline was found to be more effective than bupropion, the nicotine patch, or placebo for helping people with or without a mental health diagnosis to stop smoking. stem: A 45-year-old man with bipolar disorder has acutely increased his caffeine consumption. According to current evidence, it is clear that he is at high risk of developing a
explanation: The literature examining clinical effects of caffeine in patients with bipolar disorder is not conclusive. Acute increases in caffeine consumption may precede the occurrence of manic episodes in patients with bipolar disorder, potentially through a direct stimulant effect, affecting sleep patterns and/or the metabolism of lithium or other medications, although increases in caffeine intake could also be a consequence of an ongoing manic relapse or a prodromal sign. Further research is needed to determine whether caffeine use impacts the long-term prognosis of bipolar disorder.

stem: You are called to A and E to see a young American tourist who has taken phencyclidine (PCP). Which of the following is least likely to be present?
options: Numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain
explanation: PCP is a hallucinogen rarely seen in the UK, except as a contaminant of other drugs. It may be smoked, snorted, taken orally, or, more rarely, parenterally. People who have just taken PCP are frequently uncommunicative, appear to be oblivious, and report active fantasy production. PCP intoxication can cause vertical or horizontal nystagmus, numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain, ataxia, dysarthria, muscle rigidity, and repeated episodes of vomiting. Occasionally, users become belligerent, irrationally assaultive, suicidal, or homicidal. Seizures are very rare.

stem: Following smoking cessation, women and heavy smokers are at greatest risk for which of the following?
explanation: The reported average increased weight gain 10 years after quitting smoking is 5kg (compared with continuing smoking). stem: Delirium tremens occurs in what percentage of episodes of alcohol withdrawal?
explanation: Delirium tremens (DTs) is an acute confusional state secondary to alcohol withdrawal. It is often preceded by withdrawal symptoms; seizures may herald its onset. It occurs in approximately 5% of episodes of alcohol withdrawal. Risk factors for DTs include a long history of alcohol dependence, past history of DTs, being older, medically compromised, and poor nutritional state. DTs are characterised by a range of clinical symptoms including autonomic hyperactivity, marked agitation, clouding of consciousness, perceptual disturbances, and paranoid delusions. Mortality is 1-15%.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 590-591. Sinclair JM, O'Neill A. Update on the management of alcohol use disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Mar;26(2):82-91.

stem: What is the lifetime risk of suicide in dependent drinkers?
explanation: Suicide in those with alcohol dependence is classically quoted as a lifetime risk of 10-15%. The lifetime risk of suicide in those with alcohol problems is estimated to be 4%. Risk factors include psychiatric comorbidity, social isolation, physical ill health, repeated failed attempts at abstinence.

stem: According to ICD -11 criteria, what is the duration of features required to make a diagnosis of alcohol dependence in a non-daily drinker?
explanation: In ICD-11, features of alcohol dependence are usually evident over a period of at least 12 months, but the diagnosis may be made if the alcohol use is continuous (daily or almost daily) for at least 3 months. ICD-11 alcohol dependence has the characteristic feature of a strong internal drive to use alcohol as manifested by: 1. Impaired control over alcohol use 2. Increased priority given to use over other activities 3. Persistence of use despite harm or negative consequences
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Cerebellar degeneration has been reported to occur in up to what percentage of alcoholics?
explanation: Cerebellar degeneration is a pathologic term to describe slowly accumulating cerebellar changes caused by alcohol toxicity. Cerebellar degeneration occurs in alcoholics with and without micronutrient deficiencies and is considered the most common CNS complication, affecting an estimated 10% to 25% of alcoholics, with some studies citing a 33% incidence among alcoholics. Cerebellar ataxia is the clinical correlate to cerebellar degeneration. The characteristic presentation is a wide-based, ataxic gait and relative absence of appendicular ataxia or other cerebellar signs, such as nystagmus or dysarthria. Once cerebellar degeneration is established, aside from thiamine supplementation, treatment is largely supportive because the damage is irreversible.
reference: Hammoud N, Jimenez-Shahed J. Chronic neurologic effects of alcohol. Clinics in Liver Disease. 2019 Feb 1;23(1):141-55.

stem: Mr Z suffers from alcohol dependence syndrome of moderate severity. He is being started on a chlordiazepoxide regime. The typical regime usually lasts for
explanation: In the ‘reducing regime’ management of alcohol withdrawal, benzodiazepines are prescribed in rapidly reducing doses in order to avoid development of secondary, iatrogenic dependence, while covering the period of maximum risk. Chlordiazepoxide may be preferred for outpatient use, as it has lower abuse potential. Diazepam is often preferred for inpatient use, as it is faster-acting and can be given parenterally. For moderate alcohol dependence, a typical regime might be 10-20mg chlordiazepoxide 4 times a day, reducing gradually over 5-7 days. Note that 5-7 days’ treatment is adequate and longer treatment is rarely helpful or necessary.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 592-593. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 459.

stem: The starting dose of acamprosate in adults weighing 60 kg or more
explanation: The dosing for acamprosate is 1998mg daily (666mg three times per day) for individuals over 60kg. For those under 60kg, the dose is 1332mg daily. Acamprosate should be initiated as soon as possible after abstinence has been achieved (the BAP consensus guidelines recommend that acamprosate should be started ‘during detoxification’ because of its potential neuroprotective effect). NICE recommends that acamprosate should be continued for up to 6 months with regular (monthly) supervision. The SPC (summary of product characteristics) recommends that it is given for 1 year.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 463.

stem: The onset of delirium tremens usually occurs how many hours after the last drink?
explanation: The usual timing for onset of delirium tremens is 72-96 hours after the last drink. The classic triad of symptoms is clouding of consciousness/confusion, vivid hallucinations (particularly in visual and tactile modalities) and marked tremor. Other clinical features include autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating and fever), paranoid delusions, agitation and insomnia. Prodromal symptoms include night-time insomnia, restlessness, fear, and confusion.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 455.

stem: Which of the following is true about relapse prevention in alcohol dependence?
options: Acamprosate is not licensed for the elderly
If a patient relapses on acamprosate it must be stopped at once
Smoking is contraindicated when taking disulfiram
Acamprosate and disulfiram must not be combined
Naltrexone has no place in treating alcohol dependence
correctAnswer: Acamprosate is not licensed for the elderly
explanation: Safety and efficacy of acamprosate have not been established in patients younger than 18 years or older than 65 years. Acamprosate should not be administered to children, adolescents, or the elderly.

stem: Which term refers to 'discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication'?
explanation: Alcohol induced amnesia (also called ‘blackouts’ or ‘palimpsest’) is not included in DSM-5/ICD-11. These are discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. Patients will report a gap in their memory lasting for several hours, with global or partial amnesia for their actions during that time. The patient’s behaviour is usually characteristic of their normal behaviour when intoxicated. There is a breakdown in transfer of information from short-term to long-term storage that occurs while immediate (very brief short-term) and remote (long-term; formed prior to intoxication) memory abilities remain intact. Alcohol facilitates faster forgetting. Rapid forgetting is a hallmark of hippocampal dysfunction.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 600. Hermens DF, Lagopoulos J. Binge drinking and the young brain: A mini review of the neurobiological underpinnings of alcohol-induced blackout. Frontiers in psychology. 2018 Jan 19;9:12.

stem: A 49-year-old man is heavily dependent on alcohol. Due to various physical problems he was strongly advised to abstain. Unfortunately since his last episode of intoxication he has developed recurrent voices that frighten him. In spite of 2 months of abstinence these hallucinations have continued. Which one of the following diagnoses best suits his presentation?
explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis is a substance-induced psychotic illness that is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. In ICD-11, it is designated as ‘alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations’. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings). With continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking; in 5%, symptoms persist with abstinence.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 602. International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Mr. Z has a history of seizures and is now admitted to a medical ward for alcohol withdrawal. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed in this situation?
explanation: A meta-analysis of trials assessing the efficacy of drugs preventing alcohol withdrawal seizures demonstrated that benzodiazepines, particularly long-acting preparations such as diazepam, significantly reduced seizures de novo. A long-acting benzodiazepine is recommended as prophylaxis in those with a previous history of seizures. Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal-related seizures when used on its own or in combination with benzodiazepines.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 455.

stem: Acamprosate appears to act centrally on which of the neurotransmitter systems?
explanation: Acamprosate is a derivative of the amino acid taurine and interacts with both the glutamate system to inhibit it and with the GABA system to enhance it, a bit like a form of ‘artificial alcohol’. Thus, when alcohol is taken chronically and then withdrawn, the adaptive changes that it hypothetically causes in both the glutamate system and the GABA system create a state of glutamate overexcitement and even excitotoxicity as well as GABA deficiency. To the extent that acamprosate can substitute for alcohol in patients during withdrawal, the actions of acamprosate mitigate the glutamate hyperactivity and the GABA deficiency.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 556.

stem: A 46-year-old gentleman has been started on disulfiram for the treatment of alcohol dependence. A common side effect reported by patients taking disulfiram is
explanation: Common side effects of disulfiram include halitosis and headache. There are rare reports of psychosis and hepatotoxicity. Disulfiram can act as a helpful adjunct to therapy and allow the patient’s relatives/employers to regain confidence in their ability to remain abstinent. There is evidence for increased efficacy with supervised administration.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 598.

stem: Which of the following medications used in the setting of delirium tremens may increase the risk of seizures?
explanation: In most cases of delirium tremens, antipsychotics should not be used, or used only after large doses of benzodiazepines have failed. NICE suggests that haloperidol can be used to manage behavioural disturbance in delirium tremens, but others urge caution in view of its cardiotoxicity and propensity to provoke seizures.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 472-473.

stem: Patients with Wernicke encephalopathy show gliosis and small haemorrhages especially in which of the following brain regions?
explanation: The distribution of the lesions of Wernicke encephalopathy is characteristic and accounts for the symptoms that include disturbances of wakefulness, hypertonia, and ocular palsies. They are found in the periventricular areas, including the medial aspect of the thalamus, hypothalamus, and mamillary bodies; the periaqueductal region at the level of the third cranial nerve; the reticular formations of the midbrain, caudal portion of the corpora quadrigemina, and the floor of the fourth ventricle may also be involved. The mamillary bodies are the most frequently affected structures.
reference: Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 226.

stem: The MATCH trial is a landmark study evaluating treatment options for alcohol dependence. Which of the following is an accurate finding from the MATCH trial?
options: Impulsivity is the strongest predictor of long term drinking outcome
Binge drinkers do better with a CBT approach
Matching patients to treatment options does not make a significant impact on outcome
Younger drinkers do better with a motivational approach
At least initially, drinkers with high psychiatric morbidity do better with CBT than 12 step programmes
correctAnswer: Matching patients to treatment options does not make a significant impact on outcome
explanation: Matching is the concept of tailoring treatments to particular types of clients to increase effectiveness. There is little evidence that matching people with alcohol dependence to treatment approaches increases effectiveness. Project MATCH (Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity) by the NIAAA was the largest national multi-site RCT of alcoholism treatment matching. Clients were randomly allocated to cognitive behavioural coping-skills therapy, motivational enhancement therapy (MET), or 12-step facilitation (TSF). It revealed few matching effects. The UK Alcohol Treatment Trial (UKATT) later explored client-treatment matching in the treatment of alcohol use comparing MET with social behaviour and network therapy (SBNT). None of the five matching hypotheses were supported.
reference: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence. Updated edition 2020.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning neuroimaging in Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) is NOT true?
options: MRI is better than CT for suspected WE
MRI may show mamillary body lesions in WE
MRI cannot predict progression to Korsakoff psychosis
MRI is the most valuable method to confirm a diagnosis of WE
MRI has high sensitivity but poor specificity in WE
correctAnswer: MRI has high sensitivity but poor specificity in WE
explanation: In Wernicke encephalopathy (WE), computed tomography (CT) can show areas of reduced attenuation density at the periaqueductal grey matter and the medial portion of the thalami but, in most cases, CT findings are negative in the acute phase of WE. MRI typically shows abnormal intensity alteration in bilaterally symmetrical lesions in the paraventricular regions of the thalamus, hypothalamus, mamillary bodies, periaqueductal region and floor of the fourth ventricle. MRI has a low sensitivity of only 53% but high specificity of 93% for the diagnosis of WE, thus MRI is currently considered the most valuable method to confirm the diagnosis.
reference: Ota Y et al. Comprehensive review of Wernicke encephalopathy: pathophysiology, clinical symptoms and imaging findings. Japanese journal of radiology. 2020 Sep;38(9):809-20.

stem: An opioid receptor antagonist that is effective in blocking the 'high' of alcohol is
explanation: Naltrexone is a mu-opioid antagonist that hypothetically blocks the euphoria and ‘high’ of heavy drinking. This theory is supported by clinical trials that show that naltrexone reduces days of heavy drinking (defined as five or more drinks per day for a man and four or more for a woman) and also increases the chances of attaining complete abstinence from alcohol.

stem: Mr. Y was assessed by the drug and alcohol team, who recommended alcohol detoxification. He is a chronic smoker and has a history of a chronic respiratory disease. Which one of the following is the most suitable drug for detoxification?
explanation: In the setting of alcohol detoxification, shorter-acting benzodiazepines (e.g. oxazepam) may be preferred in those for whom over-sedation must be avoided, in people with liver disease who may not be able to metabolise long-acting agents efficiently, and in people with COPD. However, there is a greater risk of breakthrough seizures and greater potential for misuse.

stem: Which of the following is important for the prophylaxis and treatment of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
explanation: It is generally advised that patients undergoing inpatient alcohol detoxification should be given parenteral thiamine (vitamin B complex; in the UK – Pabrinex) as prophylaxis. The standard advice is one pair of Pabrinex IM high potency daily for 5 days, followed by oral thiamine and/or vitamin B compound for as long as needed (where diet is inadequate, or alcohol consumption is resumed). If Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected, the patient should be transferred to a medical unit where IV thiamine can be administered.

stem: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?
options: The hallucinations usually last less than a week
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or derogatory voices
The hallucinations persist and respond poorly to antipsychotics
The hallucinations typically occur in persons abusing alcohol for a long time
correctAnswer: The hallucinations persist and respond poorly to antipsychotics
explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis is a substance-induced psychotic illness that is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. In ICD-11, it is designated as ‘alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations’. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) in clear consciousness and while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings). With continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking. In approximately 5%, there are prolonged symptoms. Persisting symptoms can be treated with antipsychotics.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 602. International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: In the UK, what is considered as a safe limit of weekly alcohol consumption in women?
explanation: New revised low-risk drinking guidelines were published UK-wide in 2016. They proposed that to minimise health risks from alcohol, a limit of 14 units per week for both men and women who drink regularly is recommended. This constituted a reduction for men, the previous limit being 21 units per week. For those drinking up to 14 units, spreading drinking over 3 or more days is advised. Drink-free days per week are also recommended. No alcohol during pregnancy is advised as the safest approach.

explanation: Features of mild or moderate alcohol withdrawal typically last for 3-7 days after cessation of alcohol use and include autonomic hyperactivity, increased hand tremor, anxiety, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, and headache.

explanation: Detoxification in an inpatient setting, the NICE guidelines indicate, may take place over a shorter time than in the community (suggesting 14- 21 days for methadone and 7-14 days for buprenorphine) ‘as the supportive environment helps a service user to tolerate emerging withdrawal symptoms’. As in the community, a stabilisation on the dose of a substitute opioid is first achieved, followed by gradual dose reduction, with additive medications judiciously prescribed for withdrawal symptoms if and as needed.

stem: Which of the following is regarded as the most suitable screening tool in primary care settings for detecting hazardous and dependent drinking?

stem: Which of the following is a 10-item questionnaire that is useful as a screening tool for hazardous or harmful alcohol use?
explanation: The AUDIT is a 10-item questionnaire which is useful as a screening tool in those identified as being at increased risk of alcohol-related problems. Questions 1-3 address the quantity of alcohol consumed, 4-6 the signs and symptoms of dependence and 7-10 the behaviours and symptoms associated with harmful alcohol use. Each question is scored 0-4, giving a maximum total score of 40. A score of 8 or more is suggestive of hazardous or harmful alcohol use.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 454.

stem: A 34-year-old patient who has been dependent on alcohol is involved in a road traffic accident and admitted to an orthopaedic ward for multiple fractures. Which of the following is correct with respect to his clinical state?
options: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually start within 3-12 hours
The chances of experiencing delirium is highest after 5 days
He will not have a seizure unless he has a head injury
Risk of seizures is maximal from day 3 to day 5
Having withdrawal symptoms 5 days after abstinence is unusual
correctAnswer: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually start within 3-12 hours
explanation: Mild alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually start within 3-12 hours of the last drink and peak at 24-48 hours. They may last up to 14 days. Generalised seizures usually start within 12-18 hours of the last drink. They may commence before blood alcohol levels reach zero. Delirium tremens usually start 3-4 days after the last drink.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 454-455.

stem: Disulfiram inhibits which of the following enzymes?
explanation: Disulfiram acts via the irreversible inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in the accumulation of acetaldehyde. Signs and symptoms such as flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations arise if alcohol is consumed. The reaction is dose- dependent; if a large amount of alcohol is consumed, a more severe reaction may lead to hypertension, collapse, and even death.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 598.

stem: Which class of drugs is recognised as the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal?
explanation: Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment for managing alcohol withdrawal. They reduce key symptoms, withdrawal severity, and the incidence of delirium and seizures. The most commonly used benzodiazepines are diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, oxazepam, and lorazepam.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 592-593. Sinclair JM, O'Neill A. Update on the management of alcohol use disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Mar;26(2):82-91.

explanation: In Binswanger disease (Binswanger arteriopathic subcortical encephalopathy), numerous lacunar infarcts are present in the white matter and basal ganglia. This is typically seen in patients with long-standing hypertension. It is not linked to alcohol use.

stem: In the UK, which one of the following is the drug of choice in patients with an uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal syndrome?
explanation: Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal. In the UK, chlordiazepoxide is the benzodiazepine used for most patients in most centres as it is considered to have a relatively low dependence-forming potential. Some centres use diazepam. A short- acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam or lorazepam may be used in individuals with impaired liver function.

explanation: Features of stimulant withdrawal (including amphetamines, methamphetamine, and methcathinone) may include dysphoric mood (‘crash’) sometimes with suicidal ideation, irritability, fatigue, vivid & unpleasant dreams, insomnia or (more commonly) hypersomnia, increased/insatiable appetite, psychomotor agitation or retardation, and craving for amphetamine or related stimulants.

stem: Which of the following drugs should be supervised by a family member or a carer?
explanation: The therapeutic effect of disulfiram is mediated by its incompatibility with alcohol, resulting in alcohol aversion. Supervised medication optimises compliance and contributes to effectiveness. According to NICE, disulfiram should be considered in combination with a psychological intervention for patients who wish to achieve abstinence, but for whom acamprosate or naltrexone is not suitable. Treatment should be started at least 24 hours after the last drink and should be overseen by a family member.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 465-466.

stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature seen in hepatocerebral degeneration due to alcoholism?
explanation: Hepato-cerebral degeneration is a neurological syndrome consisting of various movement disorders and cognitive impairment in advanced liver cirrhosis. It is characterised by tremor, choreoathetosis, dysarthria, gait ataxia, and cognitive impairment. Orolingual dyskinesia, dystonia, and pyramidal tract signs may also be seen. Acute hepatic encephalopathy (characterised by asterixis, hyperventilation, EEG abnormalities, and alterations in consciousness) can occur before and after the onset of hepato-cerebral degeneration.
reference: Shin HW, Park HK. Recent updates on acquired hepatocerebral degeneration. Tremor and Other Hyperkinetic Movements. 2017;7:1-12. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 261.

stem: Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories through its actions at which of the following brain regions?
explanation: In alcohol induced amnesia (also called ‘blackouts’ or ‘palimpsest’), there is a breakdown in transfer of information from short-term to long- term storage that occurs while immediate (very brief short-term) and remote (long-term; formed prior to intoxication) memory abilities remain intact. Alcohol facilitates faster forgetting. Rapid forgetting is a hallmark of hippocampal dysfunction.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 600. Hermens DF, Lagopoulos J. Binge drinking and the young brain: A mini review of the neurobiological underpinnings of alcohol-induced blackout. Frontiers in psychology. 2018 Jan 19;9:12.

stem: Which one of the following is not a marker for excess alcohol consumption?
options: All the listed options are markers for excess consumption
explanation: Elevated red cell MCV, GGT, and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) are markers for excess alcohol consumption.

stem: Which of the following types of alcohol-related neurological damage has an association with red wine?
explanation: CNS myelin is vulnerable to numerous toxins. For example, a contaminant of certain homemade Italian red wines probably causes degeneration of the heavily myelinated corpus callosum, causing the Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome. Theoretically, at least, this syndrome can damage the corpus callosum enough to produce a ‘split brain syndrome’. Patients show disconnection signs and extensive cerebral dysfunction.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. pp. 129, 172, 356.

stem: A pregnant woman who has not been prescribed any medications presents with opioid dependence. Which of the following treatments should be initiated?
explanation: Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy, and stabilisation on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice. Both methadone and buprenorphine maintenance improve maternal and foetal outcomes, and substitution treatment should be offered to pregnant opioid-dependent women. Buprenorphine is associated with less severe neonatal withdrawal symptoms. However, buprenorphine should not be initiated in pregnancy because of the risk of inducing withdrawal in the foetus. There is little evidence for acute detoxification in pregnancy. Pregnant opioid-dependent women should be encouraged to access opioid maintenance treatment rather than attempt detoxification on the basis that relapse rates are high and maternal and foetal risks are greater from failed detoxification and relapse than from maintenance treatment.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 498. McAllister-Williams RH et al. British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guidance on the use of psychotropic medication preconception, in pregnancy and postpartum 2017. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 May;31(5):519-52.

stem: Mr. X is a 45-year-old man admitted to hospital with features of severe alcohol withdrawal. Laboratory investigations are arranged. Which one of the following findings is least likely to be found in his blood test results?
explanation: Commonly seen blood-based markers of excess alcohol use include anaemia, low platelets (thrombocytopenia), neutropenia, raised MCV (macrocytosis), and raised liver function tests.
reference: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 219.

stem: Mr. W is a 46-year-old man being treated for opioid dependence who took an overdose of methadone. Which drug should be administered in the event of a methadone overdose?
explanation: Opioid overdose is a preventable cause of death. This includes overdose on illicit opioids such as heroin and more recently fentanyl and oxycodone, and overdose on prescribed opioids such as methadone or buprenorphine. Opioid overdose is characterised by the triad of unconsciousness, low respiratory rate, and pin-point pupils. Cyanosis and cold, clammy skin may also be seen. Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist that can reverse opioid overdose. It is available in pre-loaded syringes that should be administered intramuscularly. Higher doses of naloxone may be needed to displace opioids of high affinity such as buprenorphine or fentanyl. Recently, concentrated intranasal naloxone has been developed as an alternative to IM naloxone.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 474-475.

stem: Mr. Smith used to drink at several places and consume various different drinks of his choice until five years ago. Now, he only drinks at home, sticking to vodka. He is exhibiting
explanation: Narrowing of the drinking repertoire occurs when the user moves from consuming a range of beverages to drinking a single type of beverage in preference to all others. Dependent drinkers will also settle into a fixed setting. Narrowing of the repertoire may help them maintain a steady level of alcohol in the blood without much fluctuation.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 574. Edwards G, Gross MM. Alcohol dependence: provisional description of a clinical syndrome. British medical journal. 1976 May 1;1(6017):1058.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with significant alcohol-related problems is not considering changing her behaviour or lifestyle. She denies that any of her problems are alcohol-related. She is in which of the following stages of change?
explanation: Six stages of change: (1) Precontemplation: not even considering changing behaviour; does not see the behaviour as a problem, minimizes and denies associated risks, and avoids information to the contrary (2) Contemplation: has become aware that the behaviour is a problem but is ambivalent about changing, and likely sees equal or more benefits than costs from the behaviour (3) Preparation: has made a decision to attempt change (4) Action: has implemented a plan and is changing the behaviour (5) Maintenance: maintaining gains made and attempting to improve areas of life that have been harmed (6) Relapse: return to previous behaviour, but with the possibility of gaining useful strategies to extend the maintenance period on the next attempt
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 575.

stem: Which of the following features is suggestive of schizophrenia instead of alcoholic hallucinosis in patients who have psychotic symptoms on a background of alcoholism?
options: Onset of alcohol drinking clearly preceding the onset of psychosis
Atypical or late age of onset of psychotic symptoms
Presence of thought disorder and affect incongruence
Recurrence of hallucinations when drinking pattern is reinstated
correctAnswer: Presence of thought disorder and affect incongruence
explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis is a substance-induced psychotic illness that is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. In ICD-11, it is designated as ‘alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations’. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings). With continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking. Evidence supporting a diagnosis of schizophrenia (or a mood disorder with psychotic symptoms) rather than alcoholic hallucinosis include psychotic symptoms preceding the onset of alcohol use, the symptoms persisting for a substantial period of time after cessation of alcohol use or withdrawal (e.g., 1 month or more), or other evidence of a pre-existing mental disorder with psychotic symptoms. Of note, some people use substances to suppress symptoms of mental disorders like schizophrenia and full symptomatic presentations only emerge upon cessation or reduction in substance use.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 602. International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Mr. X is a patient who had been alcohol abstinent for a long time but went back to his original pattern of heavy drinking in a surprisingly rapid manner after having a priming dose of alcohol. This is referred to as
explanation: ‘Reinstatement after abstinence’ is a criterion stressed by Edwards & Gross in their early description of alcohol dependence. When a user relapses to alcohol use after a period of abstinence, they are at risk of a return to the dependent pattern in a much shorter period than the time initially taken to reach dependent use. Explanations for this include: 1. Abstinence violation effect – the cognition that ‘I had a drink, so I am a drinker again’ may cause patients to reinstate a full pattern of drinking 2. Propensity to experience withdrawal symptoms may be carried over even through the period of abstinence in some individuals 3. Cues may trigger memories after a priming dose, precipitating return of compulsive drinking
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 574. Edwards G, Gross MM. Alcohol dependence: provisional description of a clinical syndrome. British medical journal. 1976 May 1;1(6017):1058.

stem: Diminished or reverse tolerance is associated with all of the following except

When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence
explanation: Diminished tolerance is a notable phenomenon in drinkers. When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence, the tolerance may revert to normal and might lead to quick intoxication. stem: Which of the following drugs used to prevent alcohol relapse appears to act centrally on the glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter systems?
explanation: Acamprosate is a derivative of the amino acid taurine and interacts with both the glutamate system to inhibit it and with the GABA system to enhance it, a bit like a form of ‘artificial alcohol’. Thus, when alcohol is taken chronically and then withdrawn, the adaptive changes that it hypothetically causes in both the glutamate system and the GABA system create a state of glutamate overexcitement and even excitotoxicity as well as GABA deficiency. To the extent that acamprosate can substitute for alcohol in patients during withdrawal, the actions of acamprosate mitigate the glutamate hyperactivity and the GABA deficiency.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 556.

stem: Sally is 10 weeks pregnant. She is on 70mg methadone daily and wants to stop taking it. What would you advise her to do?

explanation: Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy, and stabilisation on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice. Both methadone and buprenorphine maintenance improve maternal and foetal outcomes, and substitution treatment should be offered to pregnant opioid-dependent women. Buprenorphine is associated with less severe neonatal withdrawal symptoms. However, buprenorphine should not be initiated in pregnancy because of the risk of inducing withdrawal in the foetus. Changing from methadone to buprenorphine is not recommended because of the risk of foetal withdrawal. There is little evidence for acute detoxification in pregnancy. Pregnant opioid-dependent women should be encouraged to access opioid maintenance treatment rather than attempt detoxification on the basis that relapse rates are high and maternal and foetal risks are greater from failed detoxification and relapse than from maintenance treatment.

stem: Mr Y is a 55-year-old man who was admitted to the orthopaedic ward three days ago after sustaining a fracture to his right femur following a road traffic accident. He became confused, distracted and agitated in 2-3 days following surgery. Routine blood and urine tests do not indicate infection or blood loss. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: Delirium tremens (DTs) is an acute confusional state secondary to alcohol withdrawal. It is often preceded by withdrawal symptoms; seizures may herald its onset. It occurs in approximately 5% of episodes of alcohol withdrawal. Risk factors for DTs include a long history of alcohol dependence, past history of DTs, being older, medically compromised, and poor nutritional state. DTs are characterised by a range of clinical symptoms including autonomic hyperactivity, marked agitation, clouding of consciousness, perceptual disturbances, and paranoid delusions. Mortality is 1-15%.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 590-591. Sinclair JM, O'Neill A. Update on the management of alcohol use disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Mar;26(2):82-91.

stem: Following sudden cessation of alcohol in a dependent patient, the risk of seizure is high during which of the following time periods?
explanation: Mild alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually start within 3-12 hours of the last drink and peak at 24-48 hours. They may last up to 14 days. Generalised seizures usually start within 12-18 hours of the last drink. They may commence before blood alcohol levels reach zero.

stem: A woman who repeatedly presents to A&E is pregnant and a heavy abuser of heroin. She plans to breastfeed following childbirth. Which medication is/are preferable to continue if she starts breastfeeding?
explanation: Women prescribed methadone or buprenorphine should be encouraged to breastfeed even if they continue to use illicit opioids for the following reasons: - General health benefits to the mother and the infant - Specific benefits in reducing admission length and the need for intervention in neonatal abstinence syndrome - Low concentrations of methadone and buprenorphine are transferred to the infant Patients should be advised to discontinue breastfeeding gradually, as abrupt cessation can cause a delayed neonatal abstinence syndrome.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 499.

stem: After completing opioid detoxification, a man with a supportive partner is highly motivated to remain abstinent and attend follow-up appointments. Which of the following drugs is best suited in this situation?
explanation: Naltrexone has been found by NICE to a be a cost-effective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse for those who prefer an abstinence programme, are fully informed of the potential adverse effects and benefits of treatment, are highly motivated to remain on treatment, and have a partner supporting concordance.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 496.

stem: Tim is using heroin regularly. He has been tried unsuccessfully on methadone and then on buprenorphine. Choose the next best treatment option available in the UK.
explanation: Oral options other than methadone and buprenorphine, such as slow-release oral morphine preparations and dihydrocodeine, are not licensed in the UK for the treatment of opioid dependence. There is compelling evidence supporting the use of injectable diamorphine maintenance prescribing for the treatment of patients who fail to benefit from first-line opioid substitution treatment (OST). In the UK, the prescribing doctor must have a license from the Home Office to prescribe diamorphine for opioid dependence. This treatment differs from ‘injecting rooms’, that is, safe places with sterile equipment for people who use IV drugs (usually not in treatment) in that it is part of a holistic package of care with adjunctive psychosocial interventions. It is an option in cases where the individual has not responded adequately to oral OST, and in an area where it can be supported by the necessary provisions for supervised consumption. Patients are generally seen for supervised injection in a specialist facility twice a day.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 490-491.

stem: Tom is on methadone treatment for heroin addiction. He attends A&E on two occasions as he is "running out of methadone" and demands treatment. What is the best course of action?
explanation: During opioid maintenance treatment, the aim is to prevent under-dosing (risk of use of street opioids, withdrawal symptoms) and overdosing (sedation, diversion). It is possible that this man is experiencing withdrawal symptoms due to an inadequate dose of methadone and then self medicating. Patients like this should be assessed for withdrawal and, if present, methadone dosing should be adjusted accordingly.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 637.

stem: Sally is physically dependent on dihydrocodeine, which she is taking for low back pain. She wants to stop this and go back to work. What is the best course of action?
explanation: There is a growing body of evidence that opioids are harmful in the treatment of low back pain. Opioids should never be prescribed long term and clinicians should try to reduce and stop opioids if they are not improving functioning. Other strategies to manage pain should be introduced. Non-pharmacological management options include active physiotherapy, patient-initiated stretching/strengthening, aerobic activity, yoga, pilates, and core-strengthening exercises targeting postural muscles. Exercise frequency has been shown to be more important than type, duration, or intensity of exercise.
reference: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. pp. 502-503.

stem: The risk of developing alcohol problems for those with a positive family history compared to those without a family history of alcohol problems is increased by
explanation: First-degree relatives of alcoholics have double the risk of alcohol problems themselves.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 580. Haugland SH et al. Associations between parental alcohol problems in childhood and adversities during childhood and later adulthood: a cross-sectional study of 28047 adults from the general population. Substance Abuse Treatment, Prevention, and Policy. 2021 Dec;16(1):1-7.

stem: A patient is keen to stop heroin use but is anxious about experiencing withdrawal symptoms. Which of the following is best suited to support detoxification in this patient?
explanation: Of particular interest in the initiation of buprenorphine is the phenomenon of precipitated withdrawal. This occurs because buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a high receptor affinity. If it enters the brain when a full agonist (e.g. methadone or heroin) is still present, it competes for binding at the opioid receptors and replaces the full agonist. Therefore, some receptors that were previously fully simulated become partially stimulated and the patient experiences this change as opioid withdrawal. Methadone, as a full agonist, does not produce precipitated withdrawal and may be a better option for patients who are anxious about withdrawal symptoms. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 486.

stem: What percentage of patients with schizophrenia use nicotine?
explanation: Nicotine is consumed by vaping or tobacco smoking. 70-80% of those with schizophrenia regularly smoke cigarettes (with increasing numbers switching to vaping). Possible explanations for higher rates of nicotine use are as follows: smoking causes dopamine release, leading to feelings of well-being and a reduction in negative symptoms; smoking alleviates some of the side effects of antipsychotics such as drowsiness and extrapyramidal symptoms and cognitive slowing; smoking serves as a means of structuring the day (a behavioural filler); smoking arises as a result of familial vulnerability; and/or smoking may be used as a means of alleviating the deficit in auditory gaiting that is found in schizophrenia.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 871-872.

stem: A 35-year-old man states that he is currently drinking two bottles of wine a day. He is unable to cut down due to symptoms of insomnia, agitation and tremors. He is also reported to suffer from low mood, anhedonia and fatiguability. What would be the most appropriate treatment option?
explanation: Alcohol withdrawal often takes place without medical or pharmacological treatment. Alcohol withdrawal is associated with significant morbidity and mortality when improperly managed. Pharmacological assisted withdrawal (alcohol detoxification) is likely to be needed under the following circumstances: regular consumption > 15 units/day; AUDIT score > 20; there is a history of significant withdrawal symptoms.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 456.

stem: Which of the following is a mechanism of action of acamprosate in treating alcohol dependence?
options: Balancing the GABA and glutamate systems
correctAnswer: Balancing the GABA and glutamate systems
explanation: Acamprosate is a derivative of the amino acid taurine and interacts with both the glutamate system to inhibit it and with the GABA system to enhance it, a bit like a form of ‘artificial alcohol’. Thus, when alcohol is taken chronically and then withdrawn, the adaptive changes that it hypothetically causes in both the glutamate system and the GABA system create a state of glutamate overexcitement and even excitotoxicity as well as GABA deficiency. To the extent that acamprosate can substitute for alcohol in patients during withdrawal, the actions of acamprosate mitigate the glutamate hyperactivity and the GABA deficiency.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 556.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of opioid dependence would like to consider pharmacological maintenance treatment along with psychosocial interventions. Of the listed options, the most appropriate medication would be
explanation: The most recent NICE guidelines for the management of opioid dependence (2007, update 2016) recommend methadone and buprenorphine as options for maintenance therapy. The decision about which drug to use should be made on a case-by-case basis.
reference: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on methadone and buprenorphine for the management of opioid dependence. Updated edition 2016.

stem: Which of the following screening tools has only four questions?
explanation: The CAGE questionnaire is a brief screening tool used for the identification of at-risk drinking.It consists of 4 questions: Have you ever felt you should Cut back on your drinking? Has anyone ever Annoyed you by criticizing your drinking? Have you ever felt Guilty about your drinking? Have you ever had a drink early in the morning as an Eye-opener?More than 2 positive responses suggest possible at-risk drinking and should prompt further assessment.The CAGE offers no objective assessment of the frequency or quantity of alcohol use.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 582.

stem: Which of the following substances is an active ingredient of the Ethiopian plant Catha edulis, whose leaves on chewing provide amphetamine-like stimulation?
explanation: Fresh leaves of Catha edulis (or ‘Khat’), a bush native to East Africa, are used as a stimulant for their amphetamine-like effects induced by the main ingredient, cathinone. Cathinone has most of the CNS and peripheral actions of amphetamine and appears to have the same mechanism of action. Khat is chewed like tobacco and held between the cheek and gums after chewing. Because the alkaloid is metabolized rapidly, high toxic blood levels are rarely reached. Synthetic cathinones are available for illicit use in many countries.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 303.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: Mr. P has a long standing history of substance misuse and has experienced multiple strokes. Which of the following substances is most likely to have precipitated the strokes?
explanation: Stimulants such as cocaine are potent sympathomimetic drugs, causing physiological effects, including vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and elevated blood pressure through adrenergic stimulation. The combination of increased myocardial demand with constriction of coronary blood vessels can precipitate angina pectoris and even myocardial infarction. Acute hypertension associated with stimulant use can also predispose to arterial haemorrhages, such as haemorrhagic stroke or aortic dissection. Vasoconstriction can involve damage to other end organs, including the brain, kidneys, or intestines. Grand mal seizures are frequent with stimulant overdose and may occur with routine use as well.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 307.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: Which of the following is least suggestive of an opioid withdrawal state?
explanation: Pupillary dilation, not constriction, is seen in opioid withdrawal. Other opioid withdrawal symptoms include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, piloerection or gooseflesh (from which comes the term ‘cold turkey’ for the abstinence syndrome), diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia, hypertension, and tachycardia. Persons with opioid dependence seldom die from opioid withdrawal unless they have a severe pre-existing physical illness such as cardiac disease. Residual symptoms – such as insomnia, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, and a craving for opioids – can persist for months after withdrawal.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 292.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a harmful alcohol habit is ambivalent about making any changes. He is in which stage of change?
explanation:
Six stages of change: (1) Precontemplation: not even considering changing behaviour; does not see the behaviour as a problem, minimizes and denies associated

risks, and avoids information to the contrary (2) Contemplation: has become aware that the behaviour is a problem but is ambivalent about changing, and likely sees equal or more benefits than costs from the behaviour (3) Preparation: has made a decision to attempt change (4) Action: has implemented a plan and is changing the behaviour (5) Maintenance: maintaining gains made and attempting to improve areas of life that have been harmed (6) Relapse: return to previous behaviour, but with the possibility of gaining useful strategies to extend the maintenance period on the next attempt
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 575.

stem: Which of the following is most common during cocaine withdrawal?
explanation:
Features of cocaine withdrawal may include dysphoric mood (‘crash’) sometimes with suicidal ideation, irritability, fatigue, vivid & unpleasant

dreams, insomnia or (more commonly) hypersomnia, increased/insatiable appetite, psychomotor agitation or retardation, and craving for cocaine.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: In Korsakoff syndrome, the type of memory that is most affected is
explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is a largely irreversible residual syndrome, caused by severe thiamine deficiency and occurring after incomplete recovery from a Wernicke encephalopathy, predominantly in the context of alcohol abuse and malnutrition, characterised by an abnormal mental state in which episodic memory is affected out of proportion to other cognitive functions in an otherwise alert and responsive patient, whose psychological make-up may be further distinguished by executive dysfunction, flattened affect, apathy, lack of illness insight, and possibly by fantastic confabulations in the early stage. Working memory (e.g. ability to remember a sequence of numbers) is unimpaired, as is procedural and ‘emotional’ memory. Thus, the affected individual may be able to go with a psychologist to an interview room, perform adequately on working memory testing, show evidence of a new skill (e.g. mirror writing) they practised the day before, and yet later have no memory of ever having been in that room or having seen that psychologist before.
reference: Arts NJ et al. Korsakoff’s syndrome: a critical review. Neuropsychiatric disease and treatment. 2017 Nov 27. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 606-607.

stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding ICD-11’s ‘harmful pattern of use’ compared to ‘hazardous substance use’?
options: Harmful pattern of use requires a time period of 12 months, whereas hazardous pattern of use requires a time period of 1 month
In harmful pattern of use, damage has been caused to the user or others, whereas no harm has occurred in hazardous use
In both harmful pattern of use and hazardous use, harm has been caused to the user but not to others
A user can be diagnosed with both harmful pattern of use and hazardous use of the same substance simultaneously
Once users with hazardous use become aware of the risks, they quit using, whereas users with a harmful pattern continue to use
correctAnswer: In harmful pattern of use, damage has been caused to the user or others, whereas no harm has occurred in hazardous use
explanation: ICD-11 has a diagnostic code for ‘harmful pattern of use’ wherein the pattern of substance use has caused damage to a person’s physical or mental health or has resulted in behaviour leading to harm to the health of others. This pattern of use is evident over a period of at least 12 months if substance use is episodic or at least one month if use is continuous. ‘Hazardous substance use’ is a pattern of psychoactive substance use that appreciably increases the risk of harmful physical or mental health consequences to the user or to others to an extent that warrants attention and advice from health professionals but has not resulted in specific identifiable harm and therefore does not meet the diagnostic requirements for harmful pattern of use. Hazardous substance use often persists in spite of awareness of increased risk of harm to the user or others. There is no time period associated with hazardous substance use.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: The route of cocaine administration that can produce a 'high' that can last up to 15 to 30 minutes is
explanation: The duration of cocaine’s euphoric effects (‘high’) depends upon the route of administration. The faster the absorption, the more intense the ‘high’ but the shorter the duration. The high from snorting (intranasal application) is relatively slow in onset and may last 15 to 30 minutes, while that from smoking is more immediate but may last only 5 to 10 minutes.
reference: https://www.drugabuse.gov/publications/research-reports/cocaine/what-are-short-term-effects-cocaine-use
