stem: A man who has been abusing multiple substances now complains of frequent urination and passing blood in the urine. The most likely offending drug is
explanation: Ketamine is structurally similar to phencyclidine and is used as an anaesthetic. It is a unique anaesthetic, as it does not depress the reticular activating system (thus does not usually knock out consciousness completely) but reduces the cortical awareness of painful stimuli. It is taken illicitly as a sniffed powder. The use of ketamine can cause urinary tract symptoms (e.g. frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, dysuria, and haematuria). The causal agent has not been determined, but direct irritation by ketamine and/or its metabolites is a possibility. Investigations have revealed interstitial cystitis, detrusor overactivity, and decreased bladder capacity. Symptoms generally settle several weeks after stopping ketamine.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 625. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 386.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: Globally, stimulant (cocaine and amphetamines) dependence accounts for a significant proportion of what cause of death?
explanation: Globally, stimulant dependence accounts for an important number of suicides, accidental injuries, cardiovascular disease, and homicide deaths. Cocaine dependence was associated with 0.65% of suicide deaths, 0.24% of accidental injury deaths, 0.14% of cardiovascular deaths, and 0.47% of homicide deaths in 2017. Amphetamine dependence was associated with 1.23% of suicide deaths, 0.59% of accidental injury deaths, 0.48% of cardiovascular deaths, and 1.23% of homicide deaths in 2017.
reference: Farrell M et al. Responding to global stimulant use: challenges and opportunities. The Lancet. 2019 Nov 2;394(10209):1652-67. Butler AJ et al. Health outcomes associated with crack-cocaine use: Systematic review and meta-analyses. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2017 Nov 1;180:401-16.

stem: Among the following, the drug least likely to cause physical or psychological dependence is
explanation: LSD carries no risk of overdose, and physiological dependence and withdrawals do not occur.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 624.

stem: A pregnant woman in her 2nd trimester is insistent on undergoing opioid detoxification. Which one of the following is the suitable medication?
explanation: Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy, and stabilisation on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice. Detoxification in the first trimester is contraindicated due to the risk of spontaneous abortion and in the third trimester it is associated with preterm delivery, foetal distress, and stillbirth. If detoxification is requested, this is most safely achieved in the second trimester but should only be supervised by specialists with the appropriate competencies and with careful monitoring for any evidence of instability. Detoxification should be prescribed in small frequent decrements (e.g. 2-3mg of methadone every 3-5 days). Enforcing detoxification is contraindicated.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 498.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: You are asked to see a 24-year-old man in the A&E. He is attempting to withdraw from heroin. Which of the following signs suggests an an advanced opioid withdrawal state?
explanation: Opioid withdrawal symptoms may include lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, agitation, perspiration, piloerection, vomiting, shivering, yawning and dilated pupils. Muscle spasms and twitching are signs of advanced opioid withdrawal state, and get higher scores on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale.
reference: https://elsevier.health/en-US/preview/opioid-withdrawal

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: In patients using recreational drugs, which of the following features is characteristic of phencyclidine intoxication?
explanation: PCP is a hallucinogen rarely seen in the UK, except as a contaminant of other drugs. It may be smoked, snorted, taken orally, or, more rarely, parenterally. Features of PCP intoxication may include aggression, impulsiveness, unpredictability, anxiety, psychomotor agitation, impaired judgement, numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain, slurred speech, and dystonia. Physical signs include nystagmus, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, numbness, ataxia, dysarthria, and muscle rigidity. In rare instances, seizures may occur.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 624. International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: Which of the following is correct with respect to the use of LSD?
options: It is available as a prescribed drug
Onset of action is delayed for 2 hours in most subjects
explanation: LSD is a synthetic hallucinogen synthesized in 1944 by Albert Hoffman. There was early experimentation with its role in psychotherapy, but there is no current legitimate use. It is sold impregnated onto paper, in tablets, or as a powder. Effects develop 15-30 mins after ingestion and last up to 6 hours. There is no risk of OD, and physiological dependence and withdrawals do not occur.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. P. 624.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Addictions Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: Identify the correct statement regarding treatment of opioid misuse with naltrexone?
options: Fatal overdose in those who relapse is rare
It has a much shorter half life than naloxone
Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal
Combining naltrexone with psychological interventions provides limited additional benefit over naltrexone alone
Its effectiveness as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers is confirmed
correctAnswer: Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal
explanation: Evidence for the effectiveness of naltrexone as a treatment for relapse prevention in opioid misusers has been inclusive. However, naltrexone has been found by NICE to a be a cost-effective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse for those who prefer an abstinence programme, are fully informed of the potential adverse effects and benefits of treatment, are highly motivated to remain on treatment, and have a partner supporting concordance. Close monitoring is particularly important when naltrexone is initiated because of the higher risk of fatal overdose at this time. Discontinuation of naltrexone may also be associated with an increase in inadvertent overdose from illicit opioids. People taking naltrexone often experience dysphoria, which may be caused by either withdrawal from illicit drugs or by the naltrexone itself. This emphasises the importance of prescribing naltrexone as part of a care programme that includes psychosocial therapy and general support. Naltrexone has the propensity to cause a severe withdrawal reaction in patients who are either currently taking opioid drugs or who were previously taking opioid drugs and there has not been a sufficient ‘wash-out’ period. A test dose of naloxone, which has a much shorter half-life than naltrexone, may be given to the patient as an IM dose prior to starting naltrexone treatment. Patients must be advised of the risk of withdrawal before taking naltrexone.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 496.

stem: In phencyclidine intoxication, which of the following is least likely to be seen?
explanation: PCP is a hallucinogen rarely seen in the UK, except as a contaminant of other drugs. It may be smoked, snorted, taken orally, or, more rarely, parenterally. People who have just taken PCP are frequently uncommunicative, appear to be oblivious, and report active fantasy production. PCP intoxication can cause vertical or horizontal nystagmus, numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain, ataxia, dysarthria, muscle rigidity, and repeated episodes of vomiting. Occasionally, users become belligerent, irrationally assaultive, suicidal, or homicidal. Seizures are very rare.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 624. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 320.

stem: Which of the following is not a feature of opioid withdrawal?
explanation: Pupillary dilation, not constriction, is seen in opioid withdrawal. Other opioid withdrawal symptoms include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, piloerection or gooseflesh (from which comes the term ‘cold turkey’ for the abstinence syndrome), diarrhoea, yawning, fever, insomnia, hypertension, and tachycardia. Persons with opioid dependence seldom die from opioid withdrawal unless they have a severe pre-existing physical illness such as cardiac disease. Residual symptoms – such as insomnia, bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, and a craving for opioids – can persist for months after withdrawal.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 292.

stem: Which of the following could be used as a replacement therapy for a heroin user?
explanation: Suboxone is a combination preparation of buprenorphine with naloxone. This preparation may reduce the risk of diversion. The different sublingual and parenteral absorption profiles of buprenorphine and naloxone are the key factors: if used sublingually, the naloxone will have negligible effects. However, if the combined preparation is injected, the naloxone will have a substantial effect and will attenuate the effects of buprenorphine in the short term and is also likely to precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent individuals on full opioid agonists.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 490.

stem: A 36-year-old cocaine user notices that the longer he uses the drug, the more of it is needed to achieve the same effect. This is best described as
explanation: When tolerance develops, the user finds that more of the substance must be taken to achieve the same effects. Tolerance is exhibited in individuals who display no or few signs of intoxication while at a blood level in which intoxication would be evident in a non-dependent individual. In the case of drugs, the user may attempt to combat increasing tolerance by using a more rapidly acting route of administration or by choosing a more rapidly acting form of the drug.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 574. Edwards G, Gross MM. Alcohol dependence: provisional description of a clinical syndrome. British medical journal. 1976 May 1;1(6017):1058.

stem: Mr. Y is a regular drug user who presents to the A&E experiencing vivid, unpleasant dreams. He is most likely to be experiencing withdrawal from which of the following substances?
explanation: Features of stimulant withdrawal (including amphetamines, methamphetamine, and methcathinone) may include dysphoric mood (‘crash’) sometimes with suicidal ideation, irritability, fatigue, vivid & unpleasant dreams, insomnia or (more commonly) hypersomnia, increased/insatiable appetite, psychomotor agitation or retardation, and craving for amphetamine or related stimulants.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a long standing history of alcoholism presents with ataxia, nystagmus and confusion. She is admitted to the medical ward. Which one among the following drugs should be used in the management of this case?
explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute neuropsychiatric condition caused by thiamine deficiency. If Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected, the patient should be transferred to a medical unit where IV thiamine can be administered. At least two pairs of Pabrinex (parenteral B1 replacement) IV high potency (i.e. 4 ampoules) should be given 3 times daily for 3-5 days, followed by one pair of ampoules once daily for a further 3-5 days or longer (until no further response is seen).
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 461-462. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 606.

stem: Which of the following is true about the pharmacokinetics of alcohol?
options: Females have less risk of intoxication for the same units consumed when compared to males
Drinks with more than 30% alcohol content are absorbed more readily than those with less concentration
Reduced gastric motility increases blood alcohol levels
Most alcohol is excreted unchanged in urine
Gastrectomy increases the absorption of alcohol
correctAnswer: Gastrectomy increases the absorption of alcohol
explanation: The longer alcohol is exposed to gastric alcohol dehydrogenase, the greater will be its breakdown (and consequently less the blood levels). As a result, conditions that reduce gastric stay of alcohol (e.g., surgical gastrectomy) increases the chances of a rapid overshoot of alcohol in blood and intoxication. On the other hand, conditions that increase gastric stay (e.g. pyloric stenosis) may reduce acute intoxication. In fact, an increase in alcohol-related disease occurs after bariatric surgery, likely in relation to this effect. Most alcohol is broken down by the liver (85%). A small proportion (2-5%) of the alcohol absorbed is excreted unchanged in the urine, sweat or breath. Females have a higher risk of intoxication as they have only 50% of alcohol dehydrogenase that is seen in the gastric mucosa of men. Drinks with an alcohol content between 20-30% are absorbed quickest. Drinks with a further high alcohol content are absorbed more slowly as an alcohol content over 30% irritates the gastric mucosa, stimulates mucus secretion and reduces gastric emptying.
reference: Seyedsadjadi N, Acevedo MB, Alfaro R, Ramchandani VA, Plawecki MH, Rowitz B, Pepino MY. Site of Alcohol First-Pass Metabolism Among Women. JAMA network open. 2022 Mar 1;5(3):e223711-.

stem: Which of the following signs is highlighted in the ICD-11 for a diagnosis of hallucinogen intoxication?
explanation: Features of hallucinogen intoxication may include hallucinations, illusions, perceptual changes such as depersonalisation, derealisation, or synaesthesias, anxiety, depressed or dysphoric mood, ideas of reference, paranoid ideation, impaired judgement, palpitations, sweating, blurred vision, tremors, and incoordination. Physical signs may include tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, and pupillary dilatation. In rare instances, hallucinogen intoxication may facilitate suicidal ideation and behaviour.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: What is the maximum amount of alcohol per week that is advisable for a woman who is pregnant?
explanation: New revised low-risk drinking guidelines were published UK-wide in 2016. They proposed that to minimise health risks from alcohol, a limit of 14 units per week for both men and women who drink regularly is recommended. This constituted a reduction for men, the previous limit being 21 units per week. For those drinking up to 14 units, spreading drinking over 3 or more days is advised. Drink-free days per week are also recommended. No alcohol during pregnancy is advised as the safest approach.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 586.

stem: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?
options: Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium
It usually occurs in persons abusing alcohol for a long time
The hallucinations usually resolve rapidly if alcohol consumption stops
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be derogatory
The hallucinations cannot be treated with antipsychotics
correctAnswer: The hallucinations cannot be treated with antipsychotics
explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis is a substance-induced psychotic illness that is a rare complication of prolonged heavy alcohol use. In ICD-11, it is designated as ‘alcohol-induced psychotic disorder with hallucinations’. It is characterised by experiencing hallucinations (usually auditory) in clear consciousness and while sober. It usually starts with elemental hallucinations (e.g. bangs or murmurings). With continued alcohol use they become formed voices, usually derogatory. In 95% of patients, symptoms rapidly resolve on ceasing alcohol consumption, but rapidly recur on restarting drinking. In approximately 5%, there are prolonged symptoms. Persisting symptoms can be treated with antipsychotics.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 602. International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: A man with an alcohol use disorder believes that his wife is cheating on him despite the absence of any evidence supporting his claim. This is a recognised feature of
explanation: Pathological jealousy, or Othello syndrome, is a monosymptomatic delusional disorder. It is most commonly seen secondary to current or previous alcohol abuse. The content of the primary delusion is that the patient’s spouse or partner has been, or is being, unfaithful. The patient may go to great lengths to obtain ‘evidence’. There is a significant association with violence and even homicide towards supposedly unfaithful partner. It may be necessary for the couple to separate, and this advice may need to be given to the at-risk partner.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 603.

A young woman is brought to the hospital by her friend after having a seizure. On examination her blood pressure was raised with tachycardia and is noted to have congestion of her nasal mucosa. She claims to be a Hollywood starlet and says that you are preventing her from marrying someone famous. Choose... Her friend explains that she works as a prostitute to pay for her drugs An 18-year-old gentleman who gives a history of panic attacks, anxiety, and vivid flashbacks. He has recently become more withdrawn, acted inappropriately and showed cognitive difficulties. He has a Choose... conjunctival injection and a cough A young man with a history of polysubstance abuse is sweating profusely; he appears agitated and has tachycardia. He describes features of depersonalisation and claims to "see the colour red" while Choose... listening to the New York Philharmonic.

A 23-year-old woman was brought to the A& E department, and she has a history of substance misuse. She has bradycardia, hypotension, subnormal body temperature and pinpoint pupils. Choose...
correctAnswer: A young woman is brought to the hospital by her friend after having a seizure. On examination her blood pressure was raised with tachycardia and is noted to have congestion of her nasal mucosa. She claims to be a Hollywood starlet and says that you are preventing her from marrying someone famous. Her friend explains that she works as a prostitute to pay for her drugs → Cocaine intoxication, An 18-year-old gentleman who gives a history of panic attacks, anxiety, and vivid flashbacks. He has recently become more withdrawn, acted inappropriately and showed cognitive difficulties. He has a conjunctival injection and a cough → Cannabis intoxication, A young man with a history of polysubstance abuse is sweating profusely; he appears agitated and has tachycardia. He describes features of depersonalisation and claims to "see the colour red" while listening to the New York Philharmonic. → LSD intoxication, A 23-year-old woman was brought to the A& E department, and she has a history of substance misuse. She has bradycardia, hypotension, subnormal body temperature and pinpoint pupils. → Opiate intoxication
explanation:
1) Nasal congestion is suggestive of cocaine intoxication. Clinical features include increased energy, increased confidence, heightened self- esteem, euphoria, and diminished need for sleep. The Physical effects of cocaine include nasal perforation on snorting, cerebral infarctions, subarachnoid, intraparenchymal, and intraventricular hemorrhages, TIAs, Seizures (3 to 8% of A&E visits), myocardial infarctions and arrhythmias. 2) Cannabis intoxication is characterized by impaired motor coordination, euphoria, and sensation of slowed time, social withdrawal, conjunctival injection, cough, increased appetite (munchies), dry mouth and tachycardia. Impairment in motor skills remains after the euphoriant effects are gone.

3) This patient is experiencing synaesthesia, which is a feature of LSD intoxication. Clinical features include marked anxiety or depression, ideas of reference, fear of losing one's mind, paranoid ideation, subjective intensification of perceptions, depersonalization, derealization, illusions, hallucinations, synesthesias in a state of full alertness. Physical features include sweating, tachycardia, pupillary dilation, tachycardia, sweating, palpitations, blurring of vision, tremors and incoordination. 4) Opiate intoxication: Clinical features include initial euphoria, slurred speech, impairment in attention or memory, Apathy & dysphoria follows, psychomotor agitation or retardation, pupillary constriction (if pupillary dilation is seen the overdose may be very severe and anoxia has set in), drowsiness or coma.

Substance misuse (2) For each of the following clinical presentations, which one of the listed options is the most likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old lady who is on a controlled drug prescription went on a short holiday for three days and forgot to take her prescribed medication. When she returned home, she developed diarrhoea, running Choose... nose and goose flesh. On examination, she had dilated pupils and tachycardia. A 30-year-old gentleman presented to the A&E with paranoid delusions and prominent visual hallucinations of very rapid onset following ingesting of a street drug. On examination, he had Choose... tachycardia, hypertension and pupillary dilatation. A 27-year-old woman presented to the A&E in an agitated state. She has not had her anti-anxiety medication for last three days. She complains of being anxious and has insomnia. On examination, she Choose... has tachycardia and tremor.
correctAnswer: A 25-year-old lady who is on a controlled drug prescription went on a short holiday for three days and forgot to take her prescribed medication. When she returned home, she developed diarrhoea, running nose and goose flesh. On examination, she had dilated pupils and tachycardia. → Opiate withdrawal, A 30-year-old gentleman presented to the A&E with paranoid delusions and prominent visual hallucinations of very rapid onset following ingesting of a street drug. On examination, he had tachycardia, hypertension and pupillary dilatation. → Amphetamine intoxication, A 27-year-old woman presented to the A&E in an agitated state. She has not had her anti-anxiety medication for last three days. She complains of being anxious and has insomnia. On examination, she has tachycardia and tremor. → Benzodiazepine withdrawal
explanation:
1) Opiate withdrawal effects: Morphine and heroin withdrawal syndrome begins 6 to 8 hours after the last dose, peaks in 2 days and reduces in a week usually. The clinical features include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, pupillary dilation, piloerection (goose flesh), or sweating, diarrhea, yawning, fever and insomnia. 2) Amphetamine Intoxication effects: Rapid onset of psychotic symptoms is suggestive of amphetamine intoxication. Clinical features include tachycardia or bradycardia - arrhythmias may be fatal, pupillary dilation, raised or lowered blood pressure, excessive sweating or chills, nausea or vomiting, psychomotor agitation or retardation, muscular weakness, respiratory depression, chest pain, or cardiac arrhythmias. Psychological effects such as euphoria, changes in sociability, anxiety, tension, stereotyped behaviours, impaired judgment, etc. The hallmark of amphetamine-induced psychosis is the paranoia. Sensitisation is suggested to be the biological mechanism behind stimulant induced psychosis.

3) Benzodiazepine withdrawal: Features include autonomic hyperactivity, increased tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety (most prominent), grand mal seizures and kinaesthetic hallucinations reported in a few.

Alcohol-related issues (2) Choose one option for each question below

A chronic alcoholic has stopped drinking alcohol for last three days. He has been sleeping poorly, extremely anxious, agitated, shaky and is trying to catch imaginary ants all across the room Choose...

A chronic alcoholic was admitted to psychiatric ward five days ago with a history of confusion. On examination, he had severe anterograde amnesia and was confabulating. Choose...
correctAnswer: A chronic alcoholic has stopped drinking alcohol for last three days. He has been sleeping poorly, extremely anxious, agitated, shaky and is trying to catch imaginary ants all across the room → Delirium tremens, A chronic alcoholic was admitted to psychiatric ward five days ago with a history of confusion. On examination, he had severe anterograde amnesia and was confabulating. → Korsakoff's psychosis.
explanation: 1) Case 1 is Delirium Tremens: In around 5% patients suffering from alcohol withdrawal symptoms, delirium tremens may set in. In this condition, disturbed autonomic functions (pulse, temperature and blood pressure changes in either direction), clouded consciousness with hallucinations (often Lilliputian) and agitation can occur. 2) Case 2 is Korsakoff's psychosis. About 80 percent of alcoholic patients recovering from Wernicke's encephalopathy develop Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome. It is characterized by marked deficits in anterograde and to some extent retrograde episodic memory, apathy, an intact sensorium, and relative preservation of other intellectual abilities such as attention, procedural memory and working memory. (Ref: Retrieved from http://www.enetmd.com/content/alcohol-and-psychiatric-and-physical-disorders)

Alcohol history Choose one option for each clinical situation given below

A couple present to A&E and both smell of alcohol. The woman reports that her boyfriend had a fall after a quarrel and bleeding from his ears. He had worsening headache and vomiting. On examination, he has upgoing plantar, brisk reflexes and hemiparesis. He appears confused, with unilateral plantar extensor Choose... and mild weakness of the left arm. A 44-year-old man has been brought by his wife to the psychiatric clinic as he often binge drinks and forgets where he was or what he did during the episodes of drinking. Choose...

A chronic alcoholic is prescribed an antibiotic to treat suspected amoebiasis. He develops intense flushing and hypotension. Choose...

A 44-year-old gentleman stopped drinking three months ago. However, he has started hearing voices, which doesn't make any sense and are threatening to him Choose...

A 33-year-old gentleman was arrested by the police following his disturbed behaviour after consuming an only small amount of alcohol reportedly. He was agitated and confused. He 'cleared up' after sleeping for 8 hours in the prison cell. Choose...
correctAnswer: A couple present to A&E and both smell of alcohol. The woman reports that her boyfriend had a fall after a quarrel and bleeding from his ears. He had worsening headache and vomiting. On examination, he has upgoing plantar, brisk reflexes and hemiparesis. He appears confused, with unilateral plantar extensor and mild weakness of the left arm. → Extradural haemorrhage, A 44- year-old man has been brought by his wife to the psychiatric clinic as he often binge drinks and forgets where he was or what he did during the episodes of drinking. → Alcoholic memory blackouts, A chronic alcoholic is prescribed an antibiotic to treat suspected amoebiasis. He develops intense flushing and hypotension. → Disulfiram reaction, A 44-year-old gentleman stopped drinking three months ago. However, he has started hearing voices, which doesn't make any sense and are threatening to him → Alcoholic hallucinosis, A 33-year-old gentleman was arrested by the police following his disturbed behaviour after consuming an only small amount of alcohol reportedly. He was agitated and confused. He 'cleared up' after sleeping for 8 hours in the prison cell. → Pathological intoxication.
explanation:
Case 1- The patient has suffered a head injury, with possible extradural haemorrhage that can cause severe headaches, vomiting and neurological signs. Case 2 is alcoholic blackouts. Blackouts are discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. During a blackout (at the time of intoxication), remote memory is intact but patients experience specific short-term episodic memory deficit (they can talk about their childhood, etc., but cannot remember what topic the conversation is about or how did they come to where they were).

Case 3- Disulfiram reaction. Drugs like metronidazole, used for the treatment of amoebiasis, could cause this, leading to flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and hypotension. Metronidazole is considered as a deterrent agent, also called alcohol sensitizing drugs. Case 4 is Alcoholic hallucinosis. The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign and threatening. The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the untrue nature. Case 5 is Pathological intoxication, also called idiosyncratic alcohol intoxication. It is a severe behavioural reaction developing rapidly after consumption of a small amount of alcohol. Confusion, hallucinations, high psychomotor agitation, impulsive and aggressive behaviour with risk to self or others is noted; this may last for few hours and terminate in prolonged sleep.

stem:
Alcohol Abuse & Investigations For the statements given below, identify the most appropriate test for patients with alcohol abuse from the list provided:

This is a sensitive marker of alcohol abuse Choose...

This test accurately predicts recent alcohol use and can be useful in detecting relapse Choose...

This test is more specific but less useful in detecting relapse Choose...

This is the best screening tool in primary care Choose...

This forms part of the routine assessment of patients in follow-up under a supervised detoxification programme Choose...
correctAnswer: This is a sensitive marker of alcohol abuse → Gamma glutamyl transpeptidase, This test accurately predicts recent alcohol use and can be useful in detecting relapse → Carbohydrate deficient transferrin, This test is more specific but less useful in detecting relapse → Mean corpuscular volume, This is the best screening tool in primary care → AUDIT, This forms part of the routine assessment of patients in follow-up under a supervised detoxification programme → Breathalyser
explanation:
1) Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) is a sensitive marker of alcohol abuse. Levels return to normal 2-4 weeks after abstinence and, therefore, helpful in identifying those who have relapsed after treatment. 2) Carbohydrate deficient transferrin (CDT) accurately predicts recent alcohol abuse and can be useful in detecting relapse. Carbohydrate- deficient transferrin is considered to be the single most specific and sensitive test for detecting heavy alcohol use over last ten days. But due to a high degree of intersubject variability it is best to compare CDT levels with patient's baseline. 3) Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): Elevated MCV is more specific but less sensitive than GGT for alcohol abuse. Due to the long life span of RBCs (120 days), MCVs may not return to normal for 2-4 months after abstinence and so is less useful in detecting relapse. 4) In primary care, AUDIT is the best screening tool (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test). It is a 10-item questionnaire, covering quantity, frequency, inability to control drinking, withdrawal relief, loss of memory, injury and concern by others. A score of 8 or more suggest that the person is drinking to a degree that is harmful or hazardous, whereas a score of 13 or more in women and 15 or more in

men is indicative of dependent drinking. It is a very useful and widely used scale, recommended by WHO for primary care use. 5) A breathalyser allows an objective measurement of the breath alcohol and forms part of the routine assessment of patients presenting with alcohol problems or in follow-up under supervised detoxification programme.

stem:
Alcohol screening tools (1) Choose the best option for each of the statements given below

This is the most widely used screening tool for alcoholism but it does not ask about the frequency of alcohol use Choose...

A brief structured interview for general practice use Choose...

This tool was developed for detecting dependent drinkers, and the primary focus is on lifetime rather than current occurrence of alcohol related problems Choose...

Shorter version of AUDIT used in busy A&E and hospital environments Choose...

This is a measure of recent alcohol consumption and an objective measure of alcohol intoxication in A&E departments Choose...
correctAnswer: This is the most widely used screening tool for alcoholism but it does not ask about the frequency of alcohol use → CAGE questionnaire, A brief structured interview for general practice use → Alcohol use disorders identification test (AUDIT), This tool was developed for detecting dependent drinkers, and the primary focus is on lifetime rather than current occurrence of alcohol related problems → Michigan alcohol screening test (MAST), Shorter version of AUDIT used in busy A&E and hospital environments → Fast alcohol screening test (FAST), This is a measure of recent alcohol consumption and an objective measure of alcohol intoxication in A&E departments → Blood alcohol concentration
explanation:
1) CAGE is the most widely used screening tool. It is a brief screening questionnaire for the identification of at-risk drinking. But CAGE does not ask about the frequency of alcohol consumption, levels of consumption or episodes of heavy drinking, all factors that can identify patients in the earlier stages of problem drinking. 2) AUDIT also known as Alcohol use disorders identification test is designed to be used as a brief structured interview or self-report questionnaire. It is suitable for general practice use. It is a 10-item questionnaire, covering quantity, frequency, inability to control drinking, withdrawal relief, loss of memory, injury and concern by others. A score of 8 or more indicates that the person is drinking to a degree that is harmful or hazardous, whereas a score of 13 or more in women and 15 or more in men is indicative of dependent drinking. It is a very useful and widely used scale, recommended by WHO for primary care use.

3) Michigan Alcohol Screening Test MAST was developed for detecting dependent drinkers. It has 25 questions that relate to respondents self-appraisal of problems frequently associated with excessive drinking. The major drawback of MAST is that the focus is on lifetime rather than the current occurrence of alcohol- related problems. Hence, one may miss problem drinking at early stages (Nilssen & Cone, 1994). 4) The Fast alcohol screening test (FAST) was developed from AUDIT as a shorter version to use in busy A&E and hospital environments. 5) Blood alcohol concentration is a measure of recent alcohol consumption and an objective measure of alcohol intoxication in A&E departments. It is measured in mg per 100 ml blood (mg %). It correlates well with breath alcohol measured by the breathalyzer. (Ref: Retrieved from http://www.alcoolism.org/teste/testcage_en.html)

Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor Choose...

Non-selective long-acting opiate antagonist Choose...

Mu opioid receptor partial agonist Choose...

Shorter acting mu opioid antagonist Choose...
correctAnswer: Aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor → Disulfiram, Non-selective long-acting opiate antagonist → Naltrexone, Mu opioid receptor partial agonist → Buprenorphine, Shorter acting mu opioid antagonist → Naloxone
explanation:
1) Disulfiram: Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase. It leads to accumulation of acetaldehyde if alcohol is consumed producing unpleasant reactions. It is used as a prophylactic adjunctive pharmacotherapy to prevent alcohol intake in alcohol dependence.

2) Naltrexone is a longer acting opioid mu antagonist whereas naloxone is a shorter acting opioid mu antagonist. Naltrexone is used to help prevent relapse in formerly opioid-dependent patients who are detoxified and have remained opioid-free for at least a week. 3) Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist. At lower doses it has mild agonistic effects; at higher doses it has antagonistic effects. It is used sublingually as an adjunct in managing opioid dependence. 4) Naloxone is a shorter acting opioid mu antagonist.

stem:
Stages of change I Identify the most appropriate stage of behaviour change as per Prochaska and DiClemente's model

Mr. T has not made a change to his drinking behaviour. However, he has started appreciating the costs and benefits of their behaviour Choose...

It is the final stage in the cycle in patients who are successful in negotiating the previous stages Choose...

Mr. P is content with his behaviour and is unlikely to express any need for change. He is not recognising that the substance was contributing to his problems Choose...

Mr. Q has been attempting to change his problematic smoking habits for the last four weeks. Choose...

Mr. Z plans behavioural change by setting clear goals. He also assesses past achievements and failures in his life. Choose...
correctAnswer: Mr. T has not made a change to his drinking behaviour. However, he has started appreciating the costs and benefits of their behaviour → Contemplation, It is the final stage in the cycle in patients who are successful in negotiating the previous stages → Maintenance, Mr. P is content with his behaviour and is unlikely to express any need for change. He is not recognising that the substance was contributing to his problems → Pre-contemplation, Mr. Q has been attempting to change his problematic smoking habits for the last four weeks. → Action, Mr. Z plans behavioural change by setting clear goals. He also assesses past achievements and failures in his life. → Ready for action
explanation: 1) In the contemplation stage, the user may accept that there is a problem and begins to look at both the positive and negative aspects of continued drug use. The person has become aware of why the behaviour is a problem but is ambivalent about changing. In maintenance, the person has been able to sustain the change and avoid reverting to problem behaviour for a significant period. 2) In successful patients, this usually is the last stage that continues lifelong. It is a stage of maintaining gains made and attempting to improve those areas of life harmed by drug use. 3) In the pre-contemplation stage a person is not even considering changing his or her behaviour, does not see the behaviour as a problem, minimizes and denies associated risks, and avoids information to the contrary. 4) In action, the person has implemented a plan and is changing the behaviour. It is the point of motivation, where the user attempts change. A variety of routes exists by which change may be attempted, which may or may not include medical services. 5) In the ready for action stage, the person is preparing to make plans for change. It also involves planning, preparation and self-evaluation.

correctAnswer: Opioid receptor system → Heroin, GABA receptor system → Ethanol, Acetylcholine receptor system → Nicotine, Glutamate receptor system → Phencyclidine, Adenosine receptors system → Caffeine
explanation: 1) Opiates such as heroin, morphine, codeine, etc bind to specific sites in the brain labeled opioid receptors. 2) Ethanol (alcohol) acts on the GABA receptor system. It has effects on dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area and noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus. Other drugs, which have an effect on GABA receptor system, include benzodiazepines and barbiturates. 3) Nicotine has effects on the central nervous system through nicotinic receptors, which is a subclass of acetylcholine receptors. 4) Phencyclidine binds to specific receptor sites for glutamate, which is an excitatory amino acid. 5) Caffeine acts as an antagonist of the adenosine receptors, and so increases the intraneuronal cAMP. Caffeine at high doses can affect dopamine and noradrenergic neurons.

Mr. P is a 55-year-old man with alcohol dependence who has had an inpatient detoxification and is motivated to stay dry. He has a history of ischemic heart disease, diabetes and hypertension. He is keen to Choose... have a medication as an adjunct to counselling. Mr. Q is taking medication for sleeplessness prescribed by his GP. He has read that this drug has a dangerous interaction with alcohol. Identify the drug. Choose...
correctAnswer: Mr. X is a 27-year-old gentleman who presents with paranoia and persecutory ideas. He is drinking to self-medicate. He has some motivation to stop drinking → Olanzapine, Miss. Y is a 32-year old woman who comes in with her boyfriend. She has a long- standing history of alcohol dependence and is unsure if she wants to stop → Motivational interviewing, Mr. Z is a 35-year-old gentleman who has been abstinent for three months and wants to continue remaining abstinent → Disulfiram, Mr. P is a 55-year-old man with alcohol dependence who has had an inpatient detoxification and is motivated to stay dry. He has a history of ischemic heart disease, diabetes and hypertension. He is keen to have a medication as an adjunct to counselling. → Acamprosate, Mr. Q is taking medication for sleeplessness prescribed by his GP. He has read that this drug has a dangerous interaction with alcohol. Identify the drug. → Chlormethiazole
explanation:
1) This patient has psychotic symptoms and should be treated with antipsychotic medication. 2) Motivational interviewing is a technique aimed at enabling a patient to move through the stages of change to the point where action can be contemplated. The interviewer aims to aid the patient in explaining why they should change their behaviour and how this will be achieved. 3) Disulfiram can act as an adjunct to alcohol detoxification therapy and allow the patient's relatives/employers regain confidence in their ability to remain abstinent.

4) Acamprosate could be tried for patients who wish to remain abstinent from alcohol. Disulfiram is contraindicated in patients with hypertension and coronary artery disease. 5) Chlormethiazole can cause respiratory depression and, therefore, should not be used.

Newborn baby with low birth weight, small head circumference and dysmorphic facial features Choose...

Newborn baby with low birth weight, breathing difficulties, hypotonic muscles and irritability Choose...
correctAnswer: Newborn baby with low birth weight, small head circumference and dysmorphic facial features → Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, Newborn baby who is very irritable, high-pitched cry, cries a lot with shakiness, poor feeding, Sleep-wake abnormalities and vomiting → Opiate withdrawal, Newborn shows mild tremors, intermittent irritability and increased need for handling. Neonatal reflexes are normal. → Nicotine withdrawal, Newborn baby with low birth weight, breathing difficulties, hypotonic muscles and irritability → Floppy baby syndrome
explanation:
1) Foetal alcohol syndrome is the commonest non-genetic cause of learning disability. Intellectual impairment, dysmorphic facial features in

the form of low birth weight, small head circumference and disruptive behaviour is noted. 2) Opiate withdrawal: It usually begins 24-48 hours after birth, depending on the time of last dose. The essential features are hyperirritability, gastrointestinal dysfunction, respiratory distress, and vague autonomic symptoms (e.g., yawning, sneezing, mottling, fever). Tremors and jittery movements, high-pitched cries, increased muscle tone, and irritability are common. Normal reflexes may be exaggerated. Loose stools are common, leading to possible electrolyte imbalances and diaper dermatitis. 3) Nicotine withdrawal: Mild signs such as fine tremors and variations in tone; recent data indicates subtle neonatal behaviours, such as poor self-regulation and an increased need for handling. 4) Floppy baby syndrome: Babies exposed to benzodiazepines during pregnancy are at risk for the following- breathing difficulties, low birth weight, floppy muscles, unstable body temperature, alterations in heart rate/function, irritability, convulsions, etc. Prenatal exposure to Benzodiazepine can cause toxicity and withdrawal effects at birth. Flumazenil, a Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist, can reverse many

effects of BDZs and has been used in emergencies in some BDZ-exposed neonates, successfully reversing most of the above adverse effects. (Ref: Retrieved from http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/978492-clinical)

correctAnswer: A chronic alcoholic has stopped drinking alcohol for last three days. He has been sleeping poorly, extremely anxious, agitated, shaky and is trying to catch imaginary ants all across the room → Delirium tremens, A chronic alcoholic was admitted to psychiatric ward five days ago with a history of confusion. On examination, he had severe anterograde amnesia and was confabulating. → Korsakoff's psychosis.
explanation: Case 1 refers to Delirium Tremens: In around 5% patients suffering from alcohol withdrawal symptoms, delirium tremens may set in. In this condition, disturbed autonomic functions (pulse, temperature and blood pressure changes in either direction), clouded consciousness with hallucinations (often Lilliputian) and agitation can occur. Case 2 is likely to be Korsakoff's psychosis. About 80 percent of alcoholic patients recovering from Wernicke's encephalopathy develop Korsakoff's amnesic syndrome. It is characterized by marked deficits in anterograde and to some extent retrograde episodic memory. Other features include apathy, an intact sensorium, and relative preservation of other intellectual abilities such as attention, procedural memory, and working memory. (Ref: Retrieved from http://www.enetmd.com/content/alcohol-and-psychiatric-and-physical-disorders)

Withdrawal & Intoxication syndromes For each of the clinical situations described below, choose options from the given list.

A 23-year-old man with vivid unpleasant dreams and increased appetite Choose...

A 27-year-old woman with pupillary dilatation, yawning and nausea Choose...

A 19-year-old man with nystagmus, slurred speech, incoordination of movements [Choose Two] Choose...

A 20-year-old woman with pupillary dilatation, nausea and seizures Choose...

A 23-year-old man with dysphoric mood, hypersomnia, intense cravings Choose...
correctAnswer: A 23-year-old man with vivid unpleasant dreams and increased appetite → Amphetamine withdrawal, A 27-year-old woman with pupillary dilatation, yawning and nausea → Opiate withdrawal, A 19-year-old man with nystagmus, slurred speech, incoordination of movements [Choose Two] → Inhalant intoxication, A 20-year-old woman with pupillary dilatation, nausea and seizures → Amphetamine intoxication, A 23-year-old man with dysphoric mood, hypersomnia, intense cravings → Cocaine withdrawal
explanation:
The withdrawal effects of amphetamine include vivid, unpleasant dreams, hypersomnia and increased appetite. Opioid withdrawal features include nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea, pupillary dilation, piloerection (goose flesh), or sweating, nausea, diarrhea and yawning. The intoxication effects of inhalants and benzodiazepines are the same and includes dizziness, nystagmus, incoordination, slurred speech, muscle weakness and unsteady gait. Intoxication effects of amphetamines include tachycardia or bradycardia, pupillary dilation, elevated or lowered blood pressure, perspiration or chills, nausea or vomiting, muscular weakness, respiratory depression, chest pain, or cardiac arrhythmias. The CNS effects include confusion, seizures, dyskinesias, dystonias, or coma. Cocaine Withdrawal: Effects of cocaine are short-lived - rapid cessation occurs due to rapid metabolism - this can lead to repeated use. Dysphoria (crash), anhedonia, anxiety, irritability hypersomnolence, and sometimes agitation usually end within 18 hours though in heavy dependent users this can last up to a week, peaking in 3 days. The characteristic feature is an intense craving for cocaine with a striking lack

of physical withdrawal symptoms.
